source.title: Two open problems in graph theory

accepted.question_text: Let G and H be finite simple graphs with at least three vertices. If the multiset of vertex-deleted subgraphs of G is identical to the multiset of vertex-deleted subgraphs of H, must G and H be isomorphic?

evidence.quote: Reconstruction Conjecture. Let G and H be graphs on a finite vertex set with at least three vertices. Then if [Gv : v 6 VG] and [Hw : w € VH] are the same, so are G and H .

accepted.question_text: If one is given only the set of vertex-deleted subgraphs of a finite graph, with duplicate isomorphic cards removed and multiplicities forgotten, is the original graph uniquely determined by that set?

evidence.quote: As is usual in mathematics, when one problem can’t be solved, mathematicians try another related problem. It is natural to ask if graphs are set reconstructible. That is, given the collection of vertex-deleted subgraphs, remove repetitions and then try to reconstruct the original graph(s).

accepted.question_text: Let a finite simple graph G with at least four edges be represented by the collection of all edge-deleted subgraphs obtained by removing each edge of G once. Is G uniquely reconstructible from that collection?

evidence.quote: One direction that ought to prove fruitful, though it has not yet come to fruition, is edge reconstruction. Instead of removing the vertices one at a time from a graph, remove edges.

Like the vertex-deleted case, there are some small graphs which do not satisfy the obvious edge-deleted reconstruction conjecture. So we have to restrict our attention to graphs with at least 4 edges.

accepted.question_text: A graph is hypohamiltonian if it is not hamiltonian but every vertex-deleted subgraph is hamiltonian. For which integers n does there exist a hypohamiltonian graph on n vertices? In particular, does such a graph exist on 17 vertices?

evidence.quote: If Gi is not hamiltonian and Gv is hamiltonian for all v € VG, then G is said to be hypohamiltonian.
Given that we know there are an infinite number of hypohamiltonian graphs, a natural question to ask is, "Is there a hypohamiltonian graph on n vertices for every value of n?"

No-one has yet produced a hypohamiltonian graph of order 17. Given the existence of hypohamiltonian graphs for n = 15,16 and n > 18, there seems to be a good chance that there is one for n = 17. But, of course, there might not be!

accepted.question_text: What is the minimum possible number of vertices in a planar hypohamiltonian graph, where planar means drawable in the plane without edge crossings? If N is that minimum, does there exist a planar hypohamiltonian graph on every n at least N, or are some orders missing?

evidence.quote: There also exist infinitely many planar hypohamiltonian graphs. (A planar graph is one that can be drawn in the plane without any edges crossing.)

Although we know that planar hypohamiltonian graphs exist we don’t know how small (in terms of vertices) they can be. Suppose the smallest planar hypohamiltonian graph had N vertices. Does there exist a planar hypohamiltonian graph on n vertices for all n > N or are there "gaps" ?

accepted.question_text: Does there exist an infinite hypohamiltonian graph in which every vertex has finite degree; that is, a locally finite infinite hypohamiltonian graph?

evidence.quote: Infinite hypohamiltonian graphs have been considered by Thomassen [30] but none of his examples are locally finite. That is, none of them have every vertex of finite degree. Do locally finite infinite hypohamiltonian graphs exist?
